name: Sara Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Sara, thanks for joining me. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential. Can you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 27, and I'm a marketing specialist at Oakhurst Home, a furniture and homeware brand that sells sofas, lamps and rugs online and in two showrooms. I plan the seasonal catalogue, write the product pages, and set up the photo shoots in the showroom. Today was cushions: forty cushion descriptions, and every one has to sound different.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what tires you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the photo shoot days, making a room look like somewhere you'd want to come home to. What tires me out is the pay, which is on the low side, and the commute to the showroom on the ring road. My husband Liam works in his father's joinery workshop, and between us we've got less than a month's money put by, while we're hoping to start a family in a couple of years.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any AI tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Now and then. I'll get one to suggest a first draft for a dull product, like a doormat, then I fix it. I only started after two of the girls in the office had been using it for months without any problems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next scenario is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So it settles down. Honestly, that would suit me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a handy tool for the boring jobs and leave it at that. I'm not one for big opinions online. At work I'd say, right, back to the catalogue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my job's fine in that picture, but we're still stretched. Liam's dad pays him what the workshop can afford, which isn't much. We want a baby before I'm thirty, and that's what keeps me up, not computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job, using the tool for doormats and such. We'd put fifty a month aside toward a baby fund, starting in January. I'd ask my manager, Paul, whether there's a path to senior in the next couple of years, since that's more money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled. A little worried about the money, as always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you give up to find that fifty a month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The takeaway on Fridays, and my gym membership I barely use. Liam's mum would probably slip us something at Christmas too; she always does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Paul say about a path to senior?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's said maybe, which is what managers say. I'd need to run the spring catalogue on my own to show him. That's my plan for next year.

At work I'd say, right, **back to the catalogue**.
think: I think my **job's fine**, but we're stretched.
We want **a baby** before I'm thirty, which keeps me up more than computers.
do: Use the tool for **dull products** like doormats.
Put **fifty a month** into a baby fund from January.
Run the **spring catalogue** alone to earn a senior role.
feel: I feel **mostly settled**, a little worried about money.
S0.quote: We want a baby before I'm thirty, and that's what keeps me up, not computers.
fieldNote: Her mind is on **starting a family**, not on AI.
She'd use AI only for **low-stakes** tasks.
She has a **clear plan** for promotion through the spring catalogue.

steps.text: Run the Oakhurst spring catalogue alone to earn promotion
Put fifty a month into a baby fund from January
Drop the Friday takeaway and the unused gym membership

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next scenario is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing, planning, answering customers. That's a lot of what I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families need jobs they can rely on, and firms should be careful. I'd say young people should learn a trade as well as a degree. I'd keep it to friends and family, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think Oakhurst stops hiring marketing people and makes the rest of us use the AI for the product pages. I'd probably keep my job a while, but the senior role I was aiming for might never exist. That's money we were counting on for the baby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go on the company's AI course once it was running properly, because I'm not going to be the one left behind. I'd still push for the senior role, but I'd look at the joinery too. Liam's dad has said the workshop could use someone on the finishing and upholstery side, and that's real work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's the baby plan I'd worry about most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really go into the workshop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe part-time to start. I've always liked making things look nice, and upholstery's like the photo shoots but with your hands. Liam would like having me there, probably.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the baby plan, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably push it back a year, until I knew where I'd be. I hate that. But you can't plan a family on a job that might disappear.

say: I'd say families need jobs they can **rely on**.
I'd say young people should learn a **trade** as well as a degree.
think: I think Oakhurst will **stop hiring** in marketing.
The **senior role** I wanted might never exist, and we were counting on that money for the baby.
do: Take the **company AI course** once it runs properly.
Ask Liam's dad about **upholstery** work in the workshop.
Push the **baby plan** back a year.
feel: I feel **anxious**, mainly for the **baby plan**.
S1.quote: You can't plan a family on a job that might disappear.
fieldNote: She expects **fewer chances**, not instant job loss.
The **family workshop** is her quiet fallback.
Delaying a **baby** is what upsets her most, more than the job itself.

steps.text: Take Oakhurst's AI course once it runs properly
Ask Liam's dad about part-time upholstery work in the workshop
Push the baby plan back a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next scenario is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's very quick. That's our baby plan gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families and communities have to pull together, because the government won't be ready. I'd say the church should help people find work. I wouldn't go to protests.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job's gone by 2028. Product pages, catalogues, photo shoot plans, the AI does all of it. The robots for hands-on work come about 2031, so the joinery workshop would carry on a few more years, and that's where I'd go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start at the workshop on Saturdays straight away, learning upholstery from Liam's dad. When Oakhurst let me go, I'd go full-time, even for less money. We'd cut everything, and probably give up our flat and live above the workshop for a bit; there's a room there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. And sad, because I'd be putting off a child.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Living above the workshop. What would that be like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dusty and cold, honestly. It's one room and a kettle. But it's free, and we'd save hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum about putting off a baby?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum has wanted a grandchild since our wedding, and I'd have to tell her it's not happening yet. I'd say it's not forever, just till we're on our feet.

say: I'd say **families and communities** have to pull together.
I'd say the **church** should help people find work.
think: I think my **job's gone** by 2028, because the AI does pages, catalogues and shoot plans.
The **joinery workshop** carries on until robots come around 2031.
do: Learn **upholstery** at the workshop on Saturdays.
Go **full-time** there when Oakhurst lets me go.
Give up the flat and **live above** the workshop.
feel: I feel **frightened**, and sad to put off a child.
S2.quote: My mum has wanted a grandchild since our wedding, and I'd have to tell her it's not happening yet.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose her job** and moves into the family trade.
Putting off a **child** hurts more than the money.
She'd give up their flat to **live rent-free**.

steps.text: Learn upholstery at Liam's dad's workshop on Saturdays
Give up the flat and live in the room above the workshop
Put off trying for a baby until the money's steady
Lean on Liam's family for work and housing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next scenario is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a little breathing room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is when families should plan and young people should learn trades. Firms should give notice, too. I'd keep it to people I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job still goes around 2031. But five years gives me time to learn upholstery properly, and robots don't come for that until about 2034. We might even manage the baby first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Oakhurst and save, and take a part-time upholstery course at the college in a year or so, once I'd seen how the first changes go. I'd help at the workshop on Saturdays. We'd try for a baby next year as planned, while I've still got a job with maternity pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but better. I can see a way through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait a year before the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's just me. I like to see something working before I commit. If the first year shows marketing jobs going, I'll start straight away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Liam say about the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say we'll make it work, the three of us. He'd also say his dad's workshop could use a woman's eye for fabrics. He's not wrong.

say: I'd say families should **plan** and young people learn **trades**.
I'd say **firms should give notice**, and keep it to people I know.
think: I think my job **still goes** around 2031.
Five years lets me learn **upholstery** before robots, and maybe have the baby first.
do: Take a part-time **upholstery course** in a year.
Try for **a baby** next year, while I have maternity pay.
S3.quote: We'd try for a baby next year as planned, while I've still got a job with maternity pay.
fieldNote: The extra time lets her **keep the baby plan** and still retrain.
Her **steady** nature means she waits a year to see proof.
Her husband's family **workshop** shapes every plan.

steps.text: Take a part-time upholstery course at the college
Try for a baby next year while maternity pay is there

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next scenario is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a good long while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time for families to prepare and for young people to learn trades. I'd say the firms should be honest early. I'd keep it practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd stay at Oakhurst for some years, maybe get senior, and use the AI more as the others do. The end is the same, but by then I'd have time to have children and learn upholstery without rushing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push for the senior role and learn the AI tools once they're settled. We'd have our first baby in the next year or two. Later I'd train in upholstery and move into the workshop, maybe around 2032 or so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I'd sleep. It feels like a life, not a scramble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything worry you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we'd get comfortable and not prepare. Liam's dad will be retiring by then too, so the workshop might be ours to run. That's a lot to take on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would running the workshop be a good thing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It could be, if we're ready. The workshop could be our own family business, and I could do the marketing for it myself.

say: I'd say families have **time to prepare**.
I'd say firms should be **honest early**, and young people should learn trades.
think: I think I'd stay at Oakhurst and maybe **get senior**.
There'd be time for **children** and upholstery without rushing.
do: Push for the **senior role** and learn settled AI tools.
Have our **first baby** in a year or two.
S4.quote: The workshop could be our own family business, and I could do the marketing for it myself.
fieldNote: A decade lets her keep **family plans** and change jobs calmly.
Her worry is getting **comfortable** and not preparing.
Her husband's family **workshop** could become theirs.

steps.text: Push for the senior role and learn the settled AI tools

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. It would cost us the baby plan and my job at the same time. What would help is good courses in trades, and help for small family firms like Liam's dad's to take on people.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about children. Everyone talks about jobs, but people my age are deciding whether to have a family based on this.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks about jobs, but people my age are deciding whether to have a family based on this.
portrait: Sara is a **27-year-old catalogue planner** at a furniture brand, on low pay with little saved.
Her husband works in his **father's joinery**, and they hope for a baby soon.
She leans traditional and trusts **family and community** more than government.
She's **uneasy** when change is slow and **alarmed** at AGI by 2028.
Her backup is **upholstery** in the family workshop.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which would cost her job and the baby plan.
whatWouldHelp: Help for **small family firms** to take on people.
